<!-- Replace these placeholders with the final names, with the group leader first. -->
**Presenters:** Person A (leader), Person B, Person C, Person D

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, tidymodels, here, gt)
tidymodels_prefer()

# Replace 41352 with the last five digits of the group leader's student ID.
set.seed(41352)

phones <- here("data/smartphone_cleaned_v5.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE)

phones_clean <- phones |>
  mutate(
    fast_charging = if_else(fast_charging_available == 0, 0, fast_charging),
    log_price = log(price),
    brand_group = fct_lump_n(brand_name, n = 5),
    has_5g = factor(has_5g),
    has_nfc = factor(has_nfc)
  ) |>
  select(
    log_price, processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory,
    refresh_rate, fast_charging, primary_camera_rear,
    primary_camera_front, rating, battery_capacity, has_5g,
    has_nfc, brand_group
  ) |>
  na.omit()

phone_split <- initial_split(phones_clean, prop = 0.75)
phone_training <- training(phone_split)
phone_test <- testing(phone_split)

phone_recipe <- recipe(log_price ~ ., data = phone_training) |>
  step_normalize(
    processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate,
    fast_charging, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front
  ) |>
  step_pca(
    processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate,
    fast_charging, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front,
    threshold = 0.7, id = "pca"
  ) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

phone_prep <- prep(phone_recipe)

# Note: bake() returns the PCA scores and the dummy-coded regression
# predictors. The original grouping variables are retained separately below
# only for descriptive comparisons.
pc_scores <- phone_training |>
  select(has_5g, brand_group) |>
  bind_cols(
    bake(phone_prep, new_data = phone_training) |>
      select(starts_with("PC"))
  )
var_tbl <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "variance")
loading_tbl <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "coef")
```

# Dataset and research context

## Business problem

Smartphone manufacturers and retailers need to understand which combinations of
technical specifications are linked to higher prices. Many specifications are
related. For example, phones with more RAM may also have faster processors,
larger storage, and better displays. PCA summarises these related specifications
into a smaller number of meaningful components.

This is an observational analysis. The results describe associations between
specifications and price. They do not prove that a particular specification
causes a higher price.

## Dataset

The dataset contains **`r nrow(phones)` smartphone models** and **25 variables**.
These variables describe prices, ratings, hardware specifications, connectivity
features, and brands. We converted unavailable fast-charging values to zero for
phones that do not support fast charging. After removing incomplete records,
**`r nrow(phones_clean)` models** remain for the analysis.

Source: [Smartphone Models Dataset on Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/abdurrahman22224/smartphone-new-data).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-overview
#| tbl-cap: "Overview of the smartphone dataset."
overview_tbl <- tibble(
  measure = c("Number of rows", "Number of columns", "Training rows", "Testing rows"),
  value = c(nrow(phones), ncol(phones), nrow(phone_training), nrow(phone_test))
)

overview_tbl |>
  gt()
```

## Variables used

| Analysis role | Variables | Type |
|---|---|---|
| PCA inputs | `processor_speed`, `ram_capacity`, `internal_memory`, `refresh_rate`, `fast_charging`, `primary_camera_rear`, `primary_camera_front` | Numeric |
| Regression outcome | `log_price` | Numeric |
| Additional predictors | `rating`, `battery_capacity` | Numeric |
| Additional predictors | `has_5g`, `has_nfc`, `brand_group` | Categorical |

The model uses `log_price` because smartphone prices are right-skewed. Taking
the logarithm reduces the influence of extremely expensive models and makes the
regression coefficients easier to interpret as approximate percentage changes.

# Objectives and significance

## Objectives

1. Summarise related smartphone specifications into principal components and
   explain what the retained components represent.
2. Examine how the retained components, ratings, battery capacity, connectivity
   features, and brand group are associated with smartphone price.

## Why this matters

- **Manufacturers** can identify specification bundles associated with premium
  pricing and use this information when positioning new products.
- **Retailers** can compare products more consistently when setting price ranges
  and selecting models for different market segments.
- **Consumers and analysts** can compare technical specifications more easily by
  using a smaller number of meaningful dimensions.

# Exploratory data analysis

## Price distribution

```{r}
#| label: fig-price
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of smartphone prices before and after the log transformation."
price_plot_data <- phones |>
  transmute(
    price,
    log_price = log(price)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(price_plot_data, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#2C7FB8", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of models") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

The raw price distribution is strongly right-skewed. Most models are in the
lower and middle price ranges, while fewer models are premium products. The log
transformation compresses the upper tail and provides a more suitable outcome
for the regression.

## Missing values and specification correlations

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing
#| tbl-cap: "Missing values in variables used by the analysis before cleaning."
missing_tbl <- phones |>
  summarise(across(
    c(
      price, processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate,
      fast_charging, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front,
      rating, battery_capacity
    ),
    ~ sum(is.na(.x))
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  )

missing_tbl |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation
#| fig-cap: "Correlations among the numerical variables used to develop the PCA components."
pca_vars <- phones_clean |>
  select(
    processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate,
    fast_charging, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front
  )

correlation_tbl <- cor(pca_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("variable_1") |>
  pivot_longer(
    -variable_1,
    names_to = "variable_2",
    values_to = "correlation"
  )

ggplot(correlation_tbl, aes(variable_1, variable_2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#B2182B", mid = "white", high = "#2166AC",
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The correlation matrix shows that several specifications move together. This
supports the use of PCA because related technical measures can be summarised
with a smaller set of component scores.

# PCA scores across product groups

## Comparing retained component scores

The recipe retains enough principal components to explain at least 70% of the
standardised variation. The table below compares the mean component scores for
5G and non-5G models.

> **Note on the PCA workflow:** In the class recipe, `step_pca()` is applied
> before `step_dummy()`. Therefore, after `bake()`, the categorical variables
> `has_5g` and `brand_group` are represented as dummy variables rather than
> retained with their original names. We attach the original training labels
> back to the component scores only so that we can describe PC differences
> across 5G and brand groups. This does not change the PCA calculation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pc-5g
#| tbl-cap: "Mean retained principal-component scores by 5G availability."
pc_names <- names(pc_scores)[str_detect(names(pc_scores), "^PC")]

pc_by_5g <- pc_scores |>
  group_by(has_5g) |>
  summarise(
    across(all_of(pc_names), mean),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pc_by_5g |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = all_of(pc_names), decimals = 2)
```

The group with the larger mean score on a component has higher standardised
values for the original specifications that load positively on that component.
This comparison is descriptive. It shows how product groups differ in their
specification profiles, but it does not estimate a price effect by itself.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pc-brand
#| fig-cap: "PC1 scores across the grouped smartphone brands."
pc_scores |>
  ggplot(aes(brand_group, PC1, fill = brand_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Brand group",
    y = "PC1 score",
    title = "Distribution of PC1 scores by brand group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

The final interpretation of PC1 and the other retained components must use the
loading results from the PCA section. Component names should be based on the
variables with the largest absolute loadings rather than being assigned in
advance.
